summary: Cast-iron tower in Biloxi's Highway 90 median, lit 1848; kept by the Younghans family for over sixty years; automated 1939-40; city-owned and open for tours.

structures.material: cast iron shell with brick lining

access.note: Owned by the City of Biloxi; the tower is open for tours; the grounds are in the highway median

facts.agency: City of Biloxi (deeded by the Coast Guard in 1968)

events.note: Congress appropriates $12,000 for a lighthouse at Biloxi
Cast-iron tower completed in the spring of 1848 under Henry Scoles
First keeper Marcellus J. Howard appointed; light in service from 1848
The last destructive storm before 1861, referred to by keeper Mary Reynolds
Biloxi 'Home Guards' extinguish the light and seize the tower key in June 1861
Storm of 1 October 1893 (Picayune, 21 October 1893, as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Breakwater destroyed in the storm of 1 October 1893
Breakwater repaired the following year with timber and concrete
Repairs to lantern, dwelling galleries and outbuildings; tower scaled and painted
Light converted from oil to electricity
Coast Guard assumes responsibility for the light
Last keeper Joseph J. Olivier retires; the light is automated (LighthouseFriends; the nomination and the city say 1939)
Tower declared surplus and deeded to the City of Biloxi in August 1968
Keeper's dwelling destroyed by Hurricane Camille
Listed in the National Register of Historic Places on 3 October 1973
Hurricane Katrina storm surge reaches the tower in August 2005
Partial collapse of the interior brick lining
14-month, $400,000 restoration; reopened to tours in March 2010 (city) or rededicated 19 February 2010 (LighthouseFriends)
$52,000 restoration; reopened to the public (WLOX, 27 October 2026)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination and the archive give a fifth-order lens; the city's page says a fourth-order lens was installed in 1856, and LighthouseFriends says a fifth-order lens came after the Civil War. The story gives the nomination's order and flags the disagreement.

notes_for_editor: Rich station. The National Register nomination is the spine (fully read, public domain). Conflicts left in the text: Maria Younghans's retirement (31 Dec 1918 per the 1925 Bulletin and LighthouseFriends; 1920 per the nomination); Miranda's end (1929, nomination and LighthouseFriends 23 Apr 1929); the 1939 Coast Guard takeover (nomination and city) against the 1940 automation and Olivier's retirement (LighthouseFriends and the archive); the W. D. Thompson / William B. Thompson identity and dates (nomination to 1939; archive 1929-1935 then Schrieber and Olivier); the lens (fifth order per nomination and archive; the city's 1856 fourth-order lens; LighthouseFriends' fifth-order lens after the war); tower height (53 ft above grade per nomination and WJE; 64 ft per city; 48 ft per archive); 2010 reopening (March per city; rededication 19 Feb per LighthouseFriends; 2009 restoration per WLOX); tours (WLOX 9-10 a.m. daily; LighthouseFriends 'Grounds open, tower closed'); the city's statement that the light was civilian-operated 1848-1939. The Picayune of 21 Oct 1893 was not found in Chronicling America (a search for Younghans and Biloxi, 1893, returned nothing); its quotation is second-hand via LighthouseFriends and footnoted so. The archive's position for Biloxi is malformed (30 deg 39.46 min N, 88 deg 90.15 min W) and was not used; the record's coordinates match LighthouseFriends. The roster was matched by name only. The archive's 'Maria J. Reynolds' is the same keeper as the nomination's 'Mary Reynolds'. The keepers after 1940 are not in the prose. No living people are named. Wikipedia was read for leads only; its claim that the light has been kept by women for more years than any other US lighthouse is not used. The 1926 hurricane bulletin (LSB 1926 p. 38) describes the storm track but not damage to the light, so it is not used. The research date is 2026-10-27, not 2026-10-22 as the batch note says. Fact-check additions (2026-10-22 check): LighthouseFriends gives the tower as 45 feet tall and the coast's lighthouses as more than ten; both are now in the story beside the engineers' 53 ft and 13-light count.
